title: Load Balancing at the Frontend
subtitle: Route users across regions, then preserve their connections
summary: Pip routes every request to the nearest region and overloads it. Global balancing needs demand, capacity, network conditions, and connection continuity. DNS caching and packet-forwarding choices add constraints that a simple geographic map cannot show.

concepts.title: Global routing objectives
concepts.body: Pip sends a large upload to the geographically nearest site. Interactive queries favor round-trip latency, while uploads may favor throughput. Capacity, link congestion, and infrastructure health can outweigh distance. Pip chooses a less congested route when it serves the actual request better.

concepts.title: DNS steering and resolver uncertainty
concepts.body: Pip changes a DNS answer, but old traffic keeps arriving. Recursive resolvers can represent dispersed users, and cached answers delay steering changes. Resolver populations, available client-subnet information, and capacity signals improve destination estimates. Pip accounts for uncertainty in how much traffic each authoritative answer will move.

concepts.title: VIP affinity and consistent hashing
concepts.body: Pip removes one backend and nearly every connection changes destination. A virtual IP hides the pool, but stateful packets still need backend affinity. Hash-modulo membership changes remap broadly; consistent hashing limits disruption, and connection tracking can retain assignments. Pip distinguishes continuity from proof that backend load is equal.

concepts.title: Direct replies and encapsulation
concepts.body: Pip sends backend replies directly to clients to reduce load-balancer forwarding work. MAC rewriting confines backends to a shared layer-two domain. IP encapsulation permits remote backends by tunneling packets. Pip budgets outer-header MTU space because a public-link-sized packet may fragment on the internal path.

misconceptions.claim: A low DNS TTL guarantees immediate failover.
misconceptions.correction: Resolvers and clients can retain answers; DNS steering has delayed and uneven effects.

misconceptions.claim: Hashing a connection ID modulo the pool size preserves connections during resize.
misconceptions.correction: Changing the divisor remaps many IDs. Consistent hashing is designed to reduce that disruption.

scenario.title: Distribute requests across frontends
scenario.context: A global service has users near three points of presence, but one point is at capacity. DNS answers can steer new clients while existing connections remain local.

options.label: Advertise capacity-aware frontend routes
options.benefit: Routing reflects saturation and protects the overloaded point.
options.cost: Capacity signals can lag and make routing less stable.
options.consequence: The team withdraws capacity gradually and measures user latency by region.

options.label: Send all users to the nearest point
options.benefit: Nearest routing usually lowers network latency.
options.cost: Proximity alone sends too much work to the saturated point.
options.consequence: The nearest point fails during peak while another point has headroom.

scenario.debrief: Distance is only one routing input. Steer new clients toward healthy capacity, then measure the regional user experience while cached DNS answers and existing connections delay the traffic shift.

quiz.question: Why can one authoritative DNS answer redirect far more traffic than expected?
options: The resolver may reuse the cached answer for many users
The authoritative server opens a separate connection for every request
Each DNS record always corresponds to exactly one client
quiz.explanation: Recursive caching means one answer can influence a large user population.

quiz.question: What problem does consistent hashing address at a VIP?
options: Limiting connection remapping when the backend pool changes
quiz.explanation: It keeps most assignments stable when membership changes.

quiz.question: What new constraint accompanies GRE packet encapsulation?
options: All servers must share a broadcast domain
Outer headers can push packets beyond the MTU
Responses must traverse the same load balancer
quiz.explanation: Encapsulation expands the packet and therefore requires attention to internal MTU and fragmentation.

exercise.title: Plan a frontend traffic shift
exercise.prompt: A nearby region is saturated. Describe how DNS steering and VIP connection handling affect a move to another region.
